justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term outlook anchored around the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, which appeared to be in the mid-to-upper 340s range. For the one-day horizon, I placed the estimate at 348.5, essentially assuming continuation of the recent trend with minimal drift — short-term momentum and intraday mean-reversion tendencies tend to dominate at this scale, so large moves are unlikely absent a catalyst. For the one-week estimate of 350, I incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting broader market conditions that appeared constructive, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for sector rotation or macro surprises to alter direction. The one-month estimate of 353 extends that gentle upward drift further, consistent with a slow-growth, low-volatility regime assumption, though the confidence in any specific level erodes substantially over that horizon.

The width of the confidence intervals was calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility at each time horizon, scaled appropriately. At one day, a roughly ±7.5-point 90% interval reflects typical daily price fluctuation. At one week, the interval widens to ±15 points, accounting for compounding uncertainty and the possibility of a macro announcement, earnings surprise, or Federal Reserve communication shifting sentiment. The one-month interval of ±31 points is the widest because a month encompasses multiple potential inflection points — economic data releases, geopolitical developments, and shifts in risk appetite — all of which can compound into larger directional moves than any single day would suggest.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in credit conditions, an unexpected hawkish pivot from central banks, or a geopolitical shock could easily push prices 10–15% below my lower bounds within weeks. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data print, a resolution of geopolitical tensions, or a significant risk-on rotation into equities could drive prices materially above my upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter — during periods of thin trading, moves can overshoot fundamentally justified levels by a wide margin, particularly around month-end or holiday periods. These are the scenarios my intervals are not fully designed to capture, as they represent genuine structural breaks rather than normal distributional variation.
